passage: Last winter I kept finding my son Dhruv folded over his phone on the divan, chin almost on his chest, for three or four hours at a stretch. I'm Ramesh, his father, and I'll admit my first move was to shout. That got me a slammed door. Then one evening he rubbed his neck and winced, and snapped at his sister over nothing. I saw that he was tired and sore, not just rude. So I tried something else. I bought a cheap phone stand, put it on the study table at eye level, and asked if he'd stretch with me during the ad breaks of the cricket match. He rolled his eyes, but he did it. Within a couple of weeks the neck-rubbing stopped, and the snapping got rarer. He still loves his phone. He just holds his head up now.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh put the phone stand?
qa.a: On the study table, at eye level.

qa.q: What did Ramesh feel when Dhruv winced, and what did he understand?
qa.a: He felt concerned and a little sorry for shouting, seeing that Dhruv was tired and sore, not just rude.

qa.q: Which of Ramesh's changes worked, and why?
qa.a: The eye-level stand and shared stretches in the ad breaks eased Dhruv's neck without a fight, and his temper improved too.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have seen his father's shouting compared with the stretching invitation?
qa.a: The shouting felt like an attack and got a slammed door, while stretching together felt friendly, so Dhruv went along with it.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a teenager curled over a phone with a stiff neck and short temper, and breaks, stretching and an eye-level screen easing both.

passage:
Tuesday
Grew again. Uniform pants are above my ankles and everyone in 9B noticed. I've started walking with my bag held in front of me and my shoulders pulled in, like that'll make me shorter. In assembly I stood at the very back and slouched so hard my back hurt. Yamini didi saw me at the bus stop and said, "Why are you walking like a question mark?" I wanted to disappear. But on the way home she didn't tease. She said she also hated her height in school until she joined the volleyball team, and now her long arms "are a weapon". She's taking me to evening practice at the ground on Saturday. I'm scared I'll trip over my own feet. Still, I said yes.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Yamini didi say at the bus stop?
qa.a: She said, "Why are you walking like a question mark?"

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about the growth spurt, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tanvir feels awkward and self-conscious, holding the bag in front and pulling in the shoulders to look shorter.

qa.q: Why might volleyball practice help Tanvir?
qa.a: Enjoying movement where height is useful could help Tanvir feel at home in a changing body instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Yamini seem to see Tanvir's slouching?
qa.a: She recognises it from her own school years and responds with kind reassurance and an invitation rather than teasing.

grounding: Shows a teenager awkward about a growing body slumping and hiding behind a bag, and kind reassurance plus enjoyable movement offering a way to feel at home.

subtype: Long study sessions and body aches [Actor]
passage: By the ninth hour in the university library in Ankara, Elif's neck had turned to concrete. She had been hunched over her anatomy notes since breakfast, legs tucked under the chair, and a dull ache was spreading between her shoulder blades. When Rania whispered to borrow a highlighter, Elif hissed, "Can't you buy your own?" Rania blinked and went back to her seat. Elif stared at the page and saw she had taken in nothing for twenty minutes. She stood up, stiff as a plank, and walked two slow laps of the courtyard in the cold air, rolling her shoulders. Back inside, she raised her laptop on two textbooks, set a timer to stand every hour, and slid her best highlighter onto Rania's desk with a note that said sorry.

qa.q: How did Elif raise her laptop?
qa.a: She raised it on two textbooks.

qa.q: Why did Elif hiss at Rania over a highlighter?
qa.a: Elif was sore, tired and irritable after hours of hunching, so a small request felt like too much.

qa.q: Which changes eased both Elif's body and her mood?
qa.a: Walking laps of the courtyard, rolling her shoulders, raising the laptop and standing up every hour.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt when Elif snapped, and then when the note arrived?
qa.a: Rania was likely hurt and puzzled at first, then relieved and touched by the highlighter and the apology.

grounding: Shows a student whose hours of sitting bring neck and back pain that feed irritability, and short walks, stretching and position changes easing both.

subtype: Desk-bound worker feeling stiff and low [Actor]
passage:
At the cooperative bank in Tirur, Gopika sat at the same counter from ten to five, typing passbook entries with her shoulders creeping up towards her ears. By afternoon her head throbbed and her thoughts moved like jaggery in winter. "It's the stress," she told Usha, the cashier at the next counter.
"Or it's your chair," Usha said. "You haven't stood up since tea. And your screen is so low you're bowing to it."
Gopika laughed, but the next morning she put a thick ledger under the monitor and a cushion behind her back. Every hour, when the wall clock chimed, she walked to the water pot and back. By Friday the headaches were fewer and the afternoon slump had shrunk. Nothing else at the bank had changed.

qa.q: What did Gopika put under the monitor?
qa.a: A thick ledger.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel by the afternoon, and what does she blame at first?
qa.a: She feels drained and foggy with a throbbing head, and blames the stress alone.

qa.q: Which small changes lifted Gopika's energy?
qa.a: Raising the monitor, adding a cushion and walking to the water pot every hour.

qa.q: How does Usha see Gopika's afternoons?
qa.a: Usha notices that Gopika never stands and bows to a low screen, and suggests the chair is part of the problem.

grounding: Shows a desk-bound worker with tight shoulders, headaches and sluggish thoughts who blames stress alone, and small movement breaks and a better workspace lifting her energy.

subtype: Using the body to steady the mind [Response]
passage:
Sunday night.
Had the talk with Deepak today, about him taking over my room in the flat when I move out. I'd been dreading it all week. Ten minutes before, standing in the stairwell, my shoulders were up round my ears and my breath was stuck in my throat. So I did the thing from the yoga class: dropped my shoulders, pressed both feet into the floor, and breathed out slowly, longer than the in-breath, five times. It didn't make the talk easy. Deepak still got prickly about the deposit and I still stumbled once. But I didn't raise my voice, and I could actually think about what he was saying instead of just defending myself. We'll finish it next weekend. Writing this down so I remember it works.
Anirban

qa.q: Where was Anirban standing ten minutes before the talk?
qa.a: In the stairwell.

qa.q: How was Anirban feeling before the talk, and what body signs showed it?
qa.a: Anirban was dreading it and tense, with shoulders up round the ears and breath stuck in the throat.

qa.q: What did the grounding routine change, and what did it not change?
qa.a: It kept Anirban calm enough to think and not shout, but it didn't make the talk easy or settle the deposit question.

qa.q: How might Deepak have experienced the conversation?
qa.a: Deepak was prickly about the deposit, but probably found it easier to talk because Anirban stayed calm and listened.

grounding: Illustrates a person before a hard conversation dropping the shoulders, planting the feet and lengthening the out-breath, which keeps thinking calm without fixing the problem.

passage: In their village near Margao, two-year-old Maria has a brace on her left leg and a hospital card thicker than her picture book. Every second Tuesday, Nirmala, her mother, takes the early bus with her to the city clinic. But at home Maria is just Maria. She bangs pots, chases the hens on her bottom, and hears a firm "no" when she throws rice. After each clinic day, Nirmala lets her splash in the tub and sings the hen song.

qa.q: How often does Nirmala take Maria to the city clinic?
qa.a: Every second Tuesday, on the early bus.

qa.q: How does Maria seem to feel at home, judging by her play?
qa.a: She seems happy and confident, banging pots and chasing the hens like any toddler.

qa.q: What balance does Nirmala strike between care and ordinary life?
qa.a: She keeps up the clinic visits but also gives Maria play, comfort after hard days and the same rules as any child.

qa.q: What might clinic days be like for Nirmala?
qa.a: They are probably long and tiring, starting with an early bus, which is why the bath and song afterwards matter to both of them.

grounding: Shows a toddler with a long-term condition who needs extra medical care yet also gets play, comfort and normal expectations at home.

passage:
Monday: At sports hour Imran watched the others race. At pickup he asked his papa, Jeevan, "Why are my legs slow?"
Wednesday: Jeevan sat with him on the steps. "Your legs grew differently, so they tire faster. Nobody did anything wrong." Imran thought, then asked, "Will they get fast?" "Not fast. But strong in their own way."
Saturday: At the park Imran balanced on the kerb longer than his cousin and shouted, "Papa, look! I'm the best balancer!" Jeevan clapped hard.

qa.q: What did Imran ask at pickup on Monday?
qa.a: He asked, "Why are my legs slow?"

qa.q: How was Imran feeling on Saturday at the park, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, shouting that he was the best balancer.

qa.q: What did Jeevan's answer on Wednesday get right?
qa.a: It was honest and simple, told Imran nobody was to blame, and pointed to his strength without promising what isn't true.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt hearing Imran's first question?
qa.a: Jeevan was probably a little sad and careful, wanting to answer truthfully without hurting Imran's pride.

grounding: Shows a young child with a disability noticing that others run faster and asking why, and an honest simple answer plus pride in what he can do protecting his self-worth.

passage:
Monday: A new girl, Kalyani, wheeled into Class 5. Pankaj stared at her chair with its shiny rims and heard Vikram mutter, "She can't play kho-kho, so don't pick her." Pankaj said nothing, his face going warm.
Wednesday: Mrs Rao, their teacher, had noticed. In class she said, "Kalyani, would you tell us about your chair, if you like?" Kalyani grinned and showed them the brakes. Pankaj asked how fast it went. "Faster than you downhill," she said, and everyone laughed.
Friday: At break Pankaj and Kalyani invented a relay where she carried the baton round the track on her chair. Vikram asked to join. Pankaj felt proud, but he also thought about Monday, when he had kept quiet.

qa.q: What did Kalyani show the class on Wednesday?
qa.a: She showed them the brakes on her chair.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling on Monday when Vikram muttered about Kalyani?
qa.a: Pankaj felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, his face going warm, but he stayed silent.

qa.q: How did Mrs Rao help the class?
qa.a: She modelled respectful curiosity by inviting Kalyani to share only if she wanted, which turned staring into friendly questions.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have experienced her first week?
qa.a: She may have felt shut out on Monday, then more welcome once classmates asked real questions and played with her.

grounding: Shows a classmate watching children stare at and exclude a disabled peer, and a teacher modelling respectful curiosity that leads to inclusion.

subtype: Missing school and friends because of illness [Actor]
passage:
Tuesday: From her hospital bed Arohi could hear the ward trolley squeak. Her class was doing the science fair without her. She turned her face to the wall and didn't answer Mummy.
Friday: A voice note came from Pema: "We named the volcano after you! Miss says you can do the report part from home." Arohi played it three times and smiled for the first time that week.
Next Monday: Back home, Arohi wrote the volcano report in bed, with Miss's shorter worksheet beside her. On the video call Pema held up the fizzing volcano, and Arohi's name was on the label.

qa.q: What did Pema's class name after Arohi?
qa.a: They named the volcano after Arohi.

qa.q: How was Arohi feeling on Tuesday in the hospital, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left behind; she turned her face to the wall and wouldn't answer Mummy.

qa.q: What helped Arohi stay connected to her class?
qa.a: Pema's voice note, the teacher's plan for her to write the report at home with a shorter worksheet, and the video call.

qa.q: What might Pema have felt when holding up the volcano on the call?
qa.a: Pema was probably excited and glad to include Arohi, showing her name on the label.

grounding: Shows a child missing school events because of hospital stays feeling lonely, and a friend and teacher who keep in touch and adapt the work keeping her connected.

subtype: Wanting to be treated as normal [Actor]
passage: Bhupen, you asked why I used to vanish before PE. Okay. I'm Gurleen, I've had asthma since I was little, and in Class 9 I decided I was done being "the inhaler kid". I left it in my locker. When my chest got tight during the relay, I pretended I had a stitch and sat out, wheezing quietly behind the water tank. One day it got bad and Coach Sandhu found me. I expected a scene. Instead she sat down, waited till I could breathe, and asked, "What would make carrying it easier for you?" We worked it out together: a small pouch on my belt, my choice when to step out, no announcements. That same afternoon I told the school nurse too. Now I run the relay. Some days I still hate it. But it's mine to manage.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen sit out during the relay?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen leave the inhaler in the locker?
qa.a: Gurleen felt embarrassed and tired of being "the inhaler kid", and wanted to be treated as normal.

qa.q: What made Coach Sandhu's response work?
qa.a: She asked what would help instead of taking control, and they planned a belt pouch and private choices together, respecting Gurleen's dignity.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Gurleen after hearing this story?
qa.a: Bhupen would probably understand the vanishing before PE and respect Gurleen for managing it with dignity.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a long-term condition hiding symptoms and skipping treatment to avoid standing out, and support that respects choice working better than control.
